evidence.claim: At Glasgow, the Maury River once connected with the James River and Kanawha Canal, carrying passengers, pig iron and agricultural goods toward Lexington.
evidence.quote: The Maury River formed a portion of an all-water route from the Atlantic ports of Virginia to Lexington from the late 18th to the late 19th century, primarily carrying passengers, pig iron, and agricultural products.

evidence.claim: Locks and dams helped boats navigate the shallow, rocky river; the first canal boat reached Lexington in 1860.
evidence.quote: Connected to the James River and Kanawha Canal at Glasgow, a series of canals, locks and dams allowed merchant and passenger James River bateaux to travel the shallow, rocky river. The first canal boat reached Lexington in 1860.

evidence.claim: Railways later offered faster, easier transport along much of the Maury.
evidence.quote: the Richmond and Alleghany Railroad and later Shenandoah Valley Railroad both built rail lines along major portions of the river which offered faster and easier transportation.

evidence.quote: At Natural Bridge Station, SR 130 passes by the southern end of Sallings Mountain and under Norfolk Southern Railway's Roanoke District.

evidence.claim: After the gorge, US 501 crosses the James; Route 130 continues as Elon Road, passing the Blue Ridge Parkway connection and crossing the Pedlar River.
evidence.quote: US 501 crosses the James River into Bedford County to head toward Lynchburg.  SR 130 continues east as Elon Road, which veers away from the river and has a connecting ramp interchange with the Blue Ridge Parkway.

evidence.claim: Cedar Creek passes beneath a limestone arch 215 feet high, with a span of 90 feet.
evidence.quote: Natural Bridge is a geological formation in Rockbridge County, Virginia, United States, comprising a 215-foot-high (66 m) natural arch with a span of 90 feet (27 m).

evidence.claim: Edgar W. Spencer’s explanation makes the bridge the surviving roof of an underground river tunnel that collapsed through weathering and erosion.
evidence.quote: According to Spencer, the Natural Bridge was the remnant of an underground river tunnel that diverted water to the south.

evidence.claim: US 11 runs across the top, where protective fences restrict the view beyond the roadway.
evidence.quote: U.S. Route 11 (Lee Highway) runs on top of the bridge, but protective fences make it difficult to see anything besides the roadway.

evidence.claim: The state park’s trail follows Cedar Creek under the bridge and includes Lace Falls, a 30-foot waterfall.
evidence.quote: The state park includes several long-standing attractions, including the trail under the bridge along Cedar Creek and the 30-foot-tall (9.1 m) Lace Falls.

evidence.claim: Cedar Creek passes beneath a limestone arch
evidence.quote: Consisting of horizontal limestone strata, Natural Bridge is the remains of the roof of a cave or tunnel through which the Cedar Creek once flowed.

evidence.claim: the surviving roof of an underground river tunnel that collapsed through weathering and erosion
evidence.quote: Over time, through weathering and erosion, the underground river collapsed and disappeared almost completely, the Natural Bridge being the only surviving relic of the roof of the ancient underground river.

evidence.claim: Glasgow grew quickly at the meeting of the James and Maury rivers, then suffered an equally abrupt reversal.
evidence.quote: Glasgow is a town in Rockbridge County, Virginia, United States, at the confluence of the James and Maury Rivers.

evidence.claim: When the Rockbridge Company held its drawing of lots in March 1890, only two houses stood here and the population was twenty.
evidence.quote: Glasgow was established on March 5, 1890, when the Rockbridge Company held a drawing of lots. At that time only two houses, Union Ridge and the Salling home, stood in Glasgow, which then had a population of only 20 people.

evidence.claim: By 1892, the town had paved roads, streetlamps, telephone service and a 200-room hotel.
evidence.quote: By 1892, the town had paved roads, streetlamps, telephone service and a 200-room hotel, the Rockbridge Hotel.

evidence.claim: The panic of 1893 bankrupted the company.
evidence.quote: The panic of 1893, however, led to an economic collapse that put the Rockbridge Company out of business.

evidence.claim: Most buildings in the historic district date from the 1890s, retaining evidence of that brief building surge.
evidence.quote: It includes a variety of residential, commercial, and institutional buildings dating from the 1820s to 1920s, with most structures from the 1890s.

evidence.quote: To the south of the river the peaks of the James River Face Wilderness dominate and to the north the peaks of Big Rocky Row and Little Rocky Row Mountains form a dramatic backdrop to the river far below.

flags: The saved Virginia Byways list lacks its route table. The designation is confirmed in 00.txt, but the January 15, 1987 date and a route-specific agency rationale are not available. No road-construction history is cached; corridor transport history supplies the historical paragraph.

The catalog name ends at Elon, but both catalog scope and 00.txt carry the scenic designation to US 29 Business near Madison Heights; the overview follows that full extent. No drive time is available.

Natural Bridge’s cave-roof origin is presented as Spencer’s explanation, preserving the geology section’s uncertainty. The current Washington-initials story has support only as an attributed tour-guide claim; omitted rather than promoted to fact. No primary geological or site-manager page is cached.
